mcqs.question: Two threads both execute `total = total + 1` on a shared `int total` starting at 5, with no synchronization. What is the most accurate description of the risk?
options: Both threads may read the same stale value before either writes back, so one increment is silently lost
The runtime guarantees `total` will end up incorrect only if more than two threads are involved
The compiler will refuse to compile code that increments a shared field without a lock
The risk only exists if `total` is declared `volatile`
mcqs.explanation: The read-add-write sequence isn't atomic, so two threads can both read the same value and each write back the same 'next' value, losing an increment. This can happen with just two threads; nothing about compilation forbids it; `volatile` actually helps visibility, it doesn't cause the bug.

mcqs.question: In the unsafe `Counter` class, why does `total = total + 1` create a race even though it's a single line of source code?
options: Because classes are not allowed to have private fields accessed by multiple threads
Because it compiles to separate read, add, and write steps, and another thread's operation can land in between them
Because `int` fields are always thread-safe unless explicitly marked otherwise
Because `increment()` is a public method, and public methods are inherently unsafe
mcqs.explanation: One line of source doesn't mean one atomic step at execution -- 'read, add, write' are separate operations a scheduler can interleave. There's no such restriction on private fields, `int` isn't safe by default, and public visibility has nothing to do with thread-safety.

mcqs.question: A class is documented as 'thread-safe only if the caller synchronizes externally.' What does that actually mean for someone using it?
options: The class will throw an exception if used from multiple threads without a lock
The class is a bug and should never be used in concurrent code
The caller must wrap every access to the object in the same external lock, or correctness isn't guaranteed
The class synchronizes itself the first time it detects more than one thread
mcqs.explanation: This label pushes the safety guarantee onto the caller -- every access must go through the same external lock, or you get silent corruption, not an exception. Plenty of well-designed classes (like plain `ArrayList`) work this way by design; there's no self-detecting synchronization.

mcqs.question: A class has a `containsKey(k)` method and a `put(k, v)` method, each individually thread-safe. A caller does `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)`. Why can this still race?
options: It can't race -- since both methods are individually thread-safe, any sequence of calls to them is also safe
It only races if `containsKey` and `put` are called from the same thread
It races only when the map is empty
Another thread can put the key between this thread's `containsKey` check and its `put` call, so the check-then-act sequence isn't atomic even though each method is
mcqs.explanation: Individual method safety doesn't compose into safety for a sequence of calls -- that's exactly the pitfall. Two threads can interleave between the check and the act, both seeing no key present and both inserting. This has nothing to do with the map being empty or single-threaded calls.
